interview_metadata.name: Sonia Fernandez
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born here in Houston in 1969, but my parents were both from Jalisco, Mexico, so my childhood was very much two worlds. At home we spoke Spanish, listened to mariachi and Vicente Fernandez, made tamales at Christmas, and went to Mass. Outside the house I was a Houston girl, going to public school, watching the city grow, and learning early that if I wanted to be taken seriously I had to be precise and prepared. My father worked maintenance in an industrial plant, and my mother sewed and later worked in a school cafeteria, so work was not something romantic in our house. It was what kept food on the table. I finished high school and did some community college classes, mostly math and computer basics, but I did not complete a degree because I started working full time. I got into lab support and quality control in the petrochemical industry when I was young, and I stayed because I liked numbers, checklists, and knowing whether a process was truly in control. I married my husband, Manuel, in my mid-twenties, and we raised two children here in Houston. A lot of my life has been steady: work, family, church holidays, cooking, helping my kids, and keeping the house organized. Now at 57, I am thinking seriously about retirement but not about stopping. I want to keep consulting part time, finish my Six Sigma Green Belt, tutor kids in math, and maybe travel a little more, especially to Guadalajara again and one day Barcelona.

follow_ups.question: When you think back to childhood, what is one ordinary day you remember clearly?
follow_ups.response: Saturday mornings stand out. My mother would start beans early, my father would put on music while fixing something in the garage, and I would be at the kitchen table doing schoolwork or helping fold masa for tamales if it was the season. Later we might go to a cousin's house or to church.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you to be so organized and detail-oriented?
follow_ups.response: My father, mostly. He would say, 'Measure twice, mija,' and he meant it for everything, not just tools. My mother taught me the patience part, because sewing and cooking both punish you when you rush.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yes, the biggest crossroads was after high school. I had good grades in math, but my family did not have much extra money, and I felt pressure to work. I started community college at night, but then I got a clerical job connected to a testing lab. A supervisor noticed I was careful with numbers and asked if I wanted to learn sample tracking and reporting. I could have stayed on a school path, maybe become a teacher, but I chose the job because it helped my parents and gave me a real paycheck. Over time that became my career. I learned Excel, then Access, then basic statistical reporting, and I moved from being the young woman typing results to the person checking whether the results made sense.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever wonder what would have happened if you had stayed in school full time?
follow_ups.response: I do sometimes. I think I would have liked teaching math. But I also know the job gave me confidence and a good living, so I do not carry it like a regret.

follow_ups.question: Who supported that decision at the time?
follow_ups.response: My parents supported me working, though my mother always wanted me to keep studying. Later Manuel encouraged me to take short courses and certifications when the kids were little.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was both. The first job almost just happened because I needed work, but staying in quality and data was a conscious choice. I recognized I was good at it, and I liked being the person people trusted when numbers had to be right.

follow_ups.question: What made you realize you were good at it?
follow_ups.response: I caught a duplicated batch number that everyone else missed. It was small, but the engineer thanked me in front of the team, and I thought, okay, this carefulness is worth something.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how you saw yourself?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I stopped thinking of myself as just support staff and started thinking of myself as part of the technical process.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. A stronger college advising program or a scholarship that worked for someone helping family would have made a difference. I did not know how to connect work, school, and long-term career planning back then.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have been most useful?
follow_ups.response: Someone sitting with me and saying, here are two or three realistic paths, here is what they cost, and here is how you can keep earning while moving up.

follow_ups.question: Is that part of why you tutor now?
follow_ups.response: Yes. When I tutor middle-school students, I try to show them that math is not just homework. It opens doors.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married to Manuel Fernandez. We have been married 31 years. He works in HVAC maintenance supervision, and he is more relaxed than I am, which is probably why the marriage works. We have two adult children. Our son Daniel is 32 and lives in Katy with his wife and little boy. Our daughter Elena is 29 and lives in Houston, closer to the Heights, and works in a medical office. We see Daniel's family about twice a month, more if there is a birthday or Astros game. Elena comes by often on Sundays, especially if I am cooking mole or caldo. My family is close but not in each other's pockets every day. We use WhatsApp a lot, and holidays are still big, especially Christmas, Easter, Mother's Day, and Dia de los Muertos.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Manuel usually do together during a normal week?
follow_ups.response: We eat dinner together most nights around 6:30, watch the news or a game, and on Saturdays we do errands early. He helps with the heavier garden work, though he says my herb labels are too strict.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk with your children?
follow_ups.response: Elena texts almost every day. Daniel is more practical, maybe two or three times a week, but he sends pictures of my grandson, and that keeps me happy.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My mother passed away eight years ago, and my father passed before her. I have one younger brother, Arturo, in Pasadena, Texas, and we are close enough to check in weekly, though we are both busy.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Arturo usually talk about?
follow_ups.response: Mostly family, his blood pressure, my work plans, and whether he is coming for the next holiday meal.

follow_ups.question: Do you see extended family often?
follow_ups.response: Yes, cousins mostly for big gatherings, funerals, quinceaneras, and holiday meals.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Outside family, I have a small circle. My closest friend is Teresa, who I met at work almost twenty years ago. We have lunch once or twice a month and compare books, recipes, and retirement worries. I also have women from my Spanish-language book club. We meet one Saturday a month, usually at the library or someone's home, and we read authors like Mariano Azuela or sometimes contemporary Mexican writers. At church and the community center I know people more casually. I am friendly, but I do not need a large social calendar.

follow_ups.question: What makes Teresa a close friend?
follow_ups.response: She understands the work world I am in, and she tells me the truth. If I am overthinking something, she says, 'Sonia, enough spreadsheet in your head.'

follow_ups.question: Do you socialize more in English or Spanish?
follow_ups.response: Both, but emotionally Spanish comes out with close friends and family. At work I switch back and forth.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in northwest Houston, in the 77086 area. It is not fancy, but it is practical and familiar. There are families who have been here a long time, newer immigrant families, small churches, taquerias, tire shops, apartment complexes, and older subdivisions. I like that I can get Mexican groceries, go to church, get to Beltway 8, and reach work without crossing the whole city. My street has people who wave but also keep privacy. I walk early near the community garden when the weather allows, and I know which houses have dogs and which corners collect water after heavy rain.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually shop nearby?
follow_ups.response: I go to H-E-B for most things, Fiesta or a carniceria for certain ingredients, and sometimes Costco if Manuel and I are stocking up.

follow_ups.question: What is your favorite local place?
follow_ups.response: There is a small panaderia not too far away where I buy bolillos and occasionally conchas for my grandson.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe in the daytime and cautious at night. I do not walk after dark by myself, and we keep good lights outside. There have been car break-ins nearby, but I would not say I live in fear.

follow_ups.question: What do you do to feel safer?
follow_ups.response: Porch lights, locked gates, knowing neighbors, and not leaving anything visible in the car.

follow_ups.question: Do neighbors look out for each other?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially through texts. If a strange car is sitting too long, someone usually says something.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is convenience and cultural comfort. The hard part is traffic, flooding worries, and sometimes neglected roads or drainage. Houston gives you opportunity, but it also makes you plan around weather and distance.

follow_ups.question: Has flooding affected you directly?
follow_ups.response: We have not flooded inside the house, thank God, but the street has held water, and during big storms I move important papers higher.

follow_ups.question: Would you move?
follow_ups.response: Maybe after retirement, but probably still around Houston because family is here.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is just me and my husband, Manuel. We have a three-bedroom house, but the children are grown and live on their own. One room is a guest room, and one is partly my office and partly storage for files, sewing things from my mother, and holiday decorations. Manuel is permanent here, of course. No one is staying temporarily right now.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide household chores?
follow_ups.response: I handle cooking, bills, and most organizing. Manuel handles yard equipment, repairs, and heavier cleaning, but we both do laundry and groceries.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone visit overnight?
follow_ups.response: My grandson may stay one night now and then, but not on a regular schedule.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just me and Manuel.

follow_ups.question: No temporary relatives right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that happened in the past?
follow_ups.response: Years ago a cousin stayed for a few weeks, but not recently.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Our grandson may sleep over occasionally, and Elena has stayed after late family events, but no regular part-time resident.

follow_ups.question: How often does your grandson stay?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every couple of months.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep things ready for him?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a small drawer with pajamas, books, and puzzles.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. No one who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: So the household count is stable?
follow_ups.response: Yes, two people.

follow_ups.question: Any college student still using this as home base?
follow_ups.response: No, both children have their own homes.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Monday through Friday I am up around 5:15. I make coffee, check my step count from the day before, water the herbs if needed, and leave for work around 6:30. Work is usually 7:15 to 4:00 or 4:30. Tuesdays and Thursdays I do yoga in the evening, either a class or a video at home. Wednesdays I try to do meal prep or bills. Saturday morning is errands, garden, laundry, and sometimes book club. Sunday is Mass, family meal if people are coming, and then I set up my week with a list.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 10:00, earlier if I have been on my feet all day.

follow_ups.question: What is the first thing you check in the morning?
follow_ups.response: The weather, because Houston decides your clothes and your traffic.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a senior quality assurance specialist in the petrochemical industry. My work is data review, quality documentation, process checks, training new staff, and helping engineers see where a process is drifting before it becomes a bigger problem. I work daytime hours, mostly Monday through Friday. Sometimes I stay late for an audit or a corrective action meeting. I am also studying for my Six Sigma Green Belt, so some evenings I spend an hour with training modules or practice problems.

follow_ups.question: What software do you use most at work?
follow_ups.response: Excel every day, Access still for some legacy tracking, and a little basic R when I need to check trends more cleanly.

follow_ups.question: Do you supervise people?
follow_ups.response: Not as their formal boss, but I train new technicians and analysts, and people come to me when they need the procedure explained.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep the household budget, schedule medical appointments, and help coordinate family holiday plans. I volunteer as a math tutor at a community center about twice a month, usually one-on-one with middle-school students. I also keep up the garden, mostly cilantro, epazote, rosemary, tomatoes when they survive the heat, and a few peppers. I do puzzles at night, especially Sudoku and crosswords, because it settles my mind.

follow_ups.question: How do you track the budget?
follow_ups.response: A spreadsheet with categories. Manuel teases me, but when insurance or property tax comes due, he appreciates it.

follow_ups.question: What kind of math do you tutor?
follow_ups.response: Fractions, decimals, basic algebra, and word problems. Word problems scare students until you teach them to slow down.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is adding more certification study time. I am trying to finish the Six Sigma Green Belt before the end of the year, so I block two evenings a week. I also started walking earlier because the heat has been tougher on me than when I was younger. And since my grandson is getting older, family weekends include more kid activities, not just adults sitting around the table.

follow_ups.question: What time do you walk now?
follow_ups.response: Usually before 7:00 on weekends, and sometimes 5:45 on weekdays if I wake up early.

follow_ups.question: Has studying been difficult after work?
follow_ups.response: Some nights, yes. My eyes get tired, so I use timers and do one module at a time.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are adults now, so I do not have school-year routines for them anymore. When they were young, mornings were very structured: breakfast, uniforms or clothes laid out, backpacks checked, and drop-off before work. Daniel played baseball for a while, and Elena did choir and later volunteered at church. I was the mother with the calendar on the refrigerator and color-coded notes.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with your grandson's routine?
follow_ups.response: Only occasionally. I might pick him up if Daniel and his wife have a conflict, but I am not the daily caregiver.

follow_ups.question: What did you emphasize with your kids after school?
follow_ups.response: Homework first, then activities. I wanted them to learn responsibility before relaxing.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Personally, I have had limited contact. I have been pulled over once for a brake light, and it was polite. I have called the non-emergency number about suspicious activity on the street. I respect the need for public safety, but I also know not everyone gets treated the same. In Houston you hear stories from neighbors and coworkers, especially young men of color, where a routine stop becomes humiliating.

follow_ups.question: Did your brake-light stop change how you felt?
follow_ups.response: It reminded me to stay calm and have documents ready. It was fine for me, but I know that is not everyone's experience.

follow_ups.question: Do you interact with officers at community events?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes at neighborhood meetings or safety events, but not regularly.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: After a neighbor's truck was broken into, police came and took a report, but nothing really happened after that. It made people feel like small property crimes are just documented, not solved.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your habits?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I stopped leaving even reusable bags visible in the car.

follow_ups.question: Did neighbors talk about it?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly through texts and while outside getting mail.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No one in my immediate family has been arrested, and I have not been arrested. I have a distant cousin who had a DWI years ago, but that is not someone I am close to day to day.

follow_ups.question: Did that cousin's situation affect family conversations?
follow_ups.response: Mostly as a warning not to drive after drinking, especially at family parties.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about younger relatives and police contact?
follow_ups.response: A little, yes. I tell them to be respectful but also to know their rights.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, especially in presidential and midterm elections, and I try not to skip local elections. I was raised to think voting is part of having a voice. I usually read a voter guide, check endorsements, and ask Manuel if he has looked at the ballot, though we do not always agree on everything. I vote early when I can because Election Day lines and work schedules can be unpredictable.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote by party or candidate by candidate?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Democrat, but I still look at the person, especially for judges and local offices.

follow_ups.question: Who encouraged you to vote?
follow_ups.response: My parents. They became citizens and took voting seriously because they had worked hard to belong here.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as a moderate Democrat, maybe practical Democrat. I care about working families, health care, education, immigration fairness, and environmental safety because I have worked around industry enough to know rules matter. I am not against business. My family's livelihood came from industry, and my own career did too. But I believe companies need accountability, especially when chemicals, air, water, and workers' safety are involved. On social issues, I lean tolerant. I am Catholic, so I have personal beliefs, but I do not think government should be cruel or make people's lives harder just to make a point. I worry about political shouting. I prefer people who can explain a plan and show the numbers.

follow_ups.question: Which issues feel most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Immigration, education, and health care. My parents were immigrants, my work depends on training and standards, and I have seen families delay care because of cost.

follow_ups.question: Do your religious views shape your politics?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but maybe not in the way people assume. For me Catholic teaching means dignity, family, service, and caring for the poor.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more worried about misinformation and more protective of institutions than I used to be. Years ago I thought if people had the same facts, they could at least argue in a reasonable way. Now even the facts are disputed. I have also become more aware of environmental justice because in Houston you can see how certain neighborhoods carry more industrial risk. I still think of myself as moderate, but I am less patient with politicians who deny obvious problems.

follow_ups.question: Where do you see misinformation most?
follow_ups.response: Facebook and forwarded messages. Someone sends a dramatic claim, and when you check it, half the time it is old or twisted.

follow_ups.question: Has work shaped your views on evidence?
follow_ups.response: Absolutely. In quality assurance, you do not get to say, 'I feel like the batch is fine.' You show the data.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me somewhat to a lot. I am Mexican-American, so my experience is not the same as Black Americans, but I understand being judged by accent, last name, or neighborhood. The videos and stories around policing made me sad and angry. I also had to think about how my own family talks about race, because Latino families can have prejudice too. It made me listen more carefully.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with Elena. She is more direct about these issues than I was at her age.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect how you see Houston?
follow_ups.response: Yes. Houston is diverse, but that does not mean everyone has equal treatment or equal protection.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the basic issue is accountability and human dignity. If someone is stopped or arrested, that should not become a death sentence or an excuse for disrespect. I also think police have hard jobs, but a hard job still needs standards, training, and consequences. In my work, if a process fails repeatedly, you do not blame the sample. You fix the process. That is how I think about policing too.

follow_ups.question: What reforms make sense to you?
follow_ups.response: Better training, body cameras with real review, mental health response teams, and tracking patterns of complaints.

follow_ups.question: Do you support protests?
follow_ups.response: Peaceful protest, yes. I may not be the person marching every weekend, but I respect people speaking up.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think race is still part of almost everything, even when people say they are tired of talking about it. Housing, schools, health, policing, job opportunities, it all connects. In my own life, being bilingual and Mexican-American has been an advantage sometimes and a barrier other times. At work I have had people assume I was clerical even when I was the one with the technical answer. So I think we need honest conversation, but also practical changes in schools, hiring, and health access.

follow_ups.question: Have you experienced discrimination directly?
follow_ups.response: Yes, usually subtle. People complimenting my English, mispronouncing my name after being corrected, or assuming I am there to translate instead of lead.

follow_ups.question: How do you respond in those moments?
follow_ups.response: I correct calmly and keep my work exact. I learned not to shrink.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have mostly talked with family and friends, donated a small amount once to a local justice organization, and paid more attention to local candidates. I have not joined a protest, partly because of health caution and partly because I am more private.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk with most about it?
follow_ups.response: Elena, Teresa, and sometimes my book club if the reading touches history or justice.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: Rarely. I may share a voting resource, but I avoid arguments on Facebook.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My daughter is the most vocal. She talks about racism at work and in health care, and she pushes us to use clearer language. Manuel agrees with fairness but gets uncomfortable with slogans. My son is quieter, but he worries about his own son growing up in a tense country. Among friends, there is a range. Some want reform, some think the media exaggerates, and I usually try to bring the conversation back to real examples.

follow_ups.question: Do these conversations ever create conflict?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but not terrible conflict. I try to keep my voice even.

follow_ups.question: Has your book club discussed race?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially when reading about the Mexican Revolution, class, land, and indigenous people.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I would say my health is good for my age, with things I have to watch. I have high blood pressure controlled with medication, and my doctor says I am in the prediabetes range, so I pay attention to walking, portions, and sugar. My knees get stiff, especially the right one, which is why yoga helps. I am not a marathon person, but I track my steps and try to keep a steady routine.

follow_ups.question: What is your usual step goal?
follow_ups.response: Eight thousand is my goal on workdays, ten thousand on weekends if the weather cooperates.

follow_ups.question: What foods do you limit for health?
follow_ups.response: Pan dulce, tortillas, rice portions, and sweet drinks. I still enjoy them, just measured.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Routine makes it easier. If I walk early, pack lunch, and plan dinner, I do well. What makes it hard is Houston heat, stress at work, family celebrations with rich food, and sitting too long at a computer. I also cook traditional food, and sometimes healthy versions do not taste like the memory you want.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually pack for lunch?
follow_ups.response: Leftovers, salad with chicken, beans, fruit, and water. I avoid vending machine lunches.

follow_ups.question: How do you adjust traditional recipes?
follow_ups.response: Less lard, more vegetables, smaller portions, and I skim fat from broths.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: In the past two years the main thing was the prediabetes warning and a flare-up of knee pain. The prediabetes scared me because diabetes runs in my family. I started taking walking more seriously and cut back on soda completely. The knee pain came after I overdid tennis one weekend, and physical therapy exercises helped. Nothing like surgery or a hospital stay, thank goodness.

follow_ups.question: How often do you play tennis now?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month with the over-50 group, and I stretch more before and after.

follow_ups.question: Did the prediabetes change your grocery shopping?
follow_ups.response: Yes. More vegetables, plain yogurt, nuts, and fewer sweet snacks in the pantry.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working, but it affects pacing. If my knee is bad, I take the elevator and avoid unnecessary trips across the plant. I also schedule medical appointments early so I miss less work.

follow_ups.question: Have you had to miss work for health recently?
follow_ups.response: Only routine appointments and one sick day for a bad cold.

follow_ups.question: Do coworkers know about your knee?
follow_ups.response: A few do. I do not make a big announcement about it.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes. Manuel has cholesterol issues and some back pain from years of physical work. My brother Arturo has blood pressure problems, and I remind him to take it seriously. Before my mother passed, I helped with appointments and medications, and that taught me how much caregiving is paperwork and driving. Now the biggest family health responsibility is keeping everyone on top of checkups.

follow_ups.question: Do you manage Manuel's appointments?
follow_ups.response: I remind him, but I try not to mother him too much. I do put dates on the calendar.

follow_ups.question: What was hardest with your mother's care?
follow_ups.response: Coordinating prescriptions and understanding what the doctor said when appointments felt rushed.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have insurance through my job, and that helps a lot. Still, deductibles and specialist copays make you think twice. I have delayed dental work before because it was expensive, and Manuel has stretched out physical therapy exercises at home instead of more visits. We have not gone without major care, but we do compare costs and stay in network very carefully.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust your primary doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes. She explains numbers clearly, which I appreciate.

follow_ups.question: What is most frustrating about the system?
follow_ups.response: Bills that arrive weeks later and do not clearly explain what insurance paid.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, in the informal family way. We use teas like manzanilla for stomach upset, honey and lemon for cough, and Vicks, of course, for everything if you ask the older generation. My mother believed in sobadas for muscle aches. I respect those traditions for comfort, but if something is serious, I go to the doctor. I do not mix herbs with medication without asking.

follow_ups.question: Do you still keep those remedies at home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, chamomile tea, ginger, honey, and Vicks are always around.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you those remedies?
follow_ups.response: My mother and aunts. It was just household knowledge.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
